passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel dietary supplement on fasting glucose levels in adults with prediabetes. A randomized, double‑blind, placebo‑controlled trial enrolled 180 participants, who were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) supplement (n = 60), (2) placebo (n = 60), and (3) no intervention (n = 60). After 12 weeks, fasting glucose was measured. Table 1 summarizes the mean fasting glucose (mg/dL), standard deviation (SD), and sample size for each group. The investigators hypothesized that the supplement would reduce fasting glucose relative to placebo and no‑intervention controls. The study also collected demographic data (age, sex, BMI) to assess potential confounding variables. The authors concluded that the supplement significantly lowered fasting glucose compared to placebo (p < .01) and that the effect was independent of age and BMI. These findings suggest a promising adjunctive therapy for prediabetes management.
table_data:
Variable | Mean (mg/dL) | SD | n
Supplement | 98 | 12 | 60
Placebo | 105 | 15 | 60
No‑intervention | 107 | 14 | 60
stem: Which group had the highest mean fasting glucose level?
explanation: The no-intervention group has the highest mean fasting glucose (107 mg/dL), compared with 105 for placebo and 98 for the supplement group.
trap: Placebo and no-intervention are close (105 versus 107), which makes the combined option tempting, but 107 is strictly higher.

stem: Which experimental design best tests the effect of the supplement on fasting glucose?
explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is the gold standard for testing an intervention’s efficacy, as it minimizes bias and confounding by random assignment.
trap: Some examinees select observational designs because they are easier to conduct, ignoring the need for randomization to establish causality.

stem: Which of the following is a potential confounder that the authors attempted to control for in their analysis?
explanation: Age is a known risk factor for glucose metabolism and could confound the relationship between supplement use and fasting glucose; the authors collected age data to adjust for it.
trap: Randomization and blinding are study design features, not confounders; sample size is a methodological consideration, not a confounder.

stem: Which statement best summarizes the clinical implication of this study?

options.A: The supplement is a proven cure for prediabetes.
options.B: The supplement may help reduce fasting glucose but requires larger trials for confirmation.
options.C: No intervention is superior to the supplement.
options.D: Placebo has the same effect as the supplement.

explanation: Correct: B) The supplement group had lower mean fasting glucose than placebo (98 vs 105 mg/dL, p < .01), which supports a possible benefit, but one 12-week trial cannot show a cure, so larger trials are needed. Why the others are wrong: A) One short trial cannot establish a cure. C) The no-intervention group had higher glucose (107) than the supplement group (98). D) The supplement group (98) differed from placebo (105) with p < .01.
trap: Some readers over‑interpret the results as a definitive cure (option A) or ignore the need for further research.
